To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
zinc fingers are targets of carcinogenic metals and that the damage of zinc fingers is a novel molecular mechanism of metal carcinogenesis.
the carcinogenic metals, such as arsenite, nickel and cadmium, and other putative carcinogens inhibit zinc finger containing proteins and damage or distort zinc fingers.
zinc finger motifs of DNA repair proteins are susceptible to damage by carcinogenic metals, and that the damage may be responsible for carcinogenesis in humans.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of metals and metallo-organic compounds, including carcinogens, in the inhibition of DNA repair.
the role of zinc in the function of zinc finger containing DNA binding and repair proteins.
the identification of the mechanism by which carcinogens damage zinc finger motifs and the role of zinc finger motifs in DNA repair and carcinogenesis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the damage of zinc fingers in repair proteins is a novel molecular mechanism of carcinogenesis, which can be caused by carcinogenic metals and putative carcinogenic metals, as well by oxidative substances.
zinc finger proteins can be inactivated by the action of redox-active carcinogenic metals and their compounds, and this mechanism can be regarded as a new molecular mechanism in carcinogensis.
the inhibition of zinc finger containing DNA repairing proteins is a novel molecular mechanism of carcinogenesis.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
zinc finger containing proteins are damaged by carcinogenic metal and metalloid compounds, which may be an additional factor in carcinogenesis.
the carcinogenic metals can damage zinc finger domains in DNA repair proteins.

zinc finger motifs are sensitive to the action of carcinogenic metals and oxidative substances, and that the inhibition or distortion of zinc finger containing proteins, including DNA repair enzymes, may be a novel mechanism in the development of cancer.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the carcinogenicity of metals, such as arsenite, cadmium, cobalt, nickel and lead, may be due to their ability to interact with zinc finger containing DNA damage repair proteins.
metals and metalloidal compounds can damage DNA repair proteins, and this is an additional mechanism of metal carcinogenesis, in addition to their ability to damage DNA.
the reactivity of zinc finger containing proteins towards redox active metals and other oxidative agents may be a novel molecular mechanism of metal and metalloid carcinogenicity.
